passages.happening:
“From the blue, purple, and scarlet yarn they made specially woven garments for ministry in the sanctuary, as well as the holy garments for Aaron, just as the LORD had commanded Moses” (verse 1).

The ephod is made of fine linen with gold worked into it (verses 2-5). “They mounted the onyx stones in gold filigree settings, engraved like a seal with the names of the sons of Israel. Then they fastened them on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as memorial stones for the sons of Israel” (verses 6-7).

The breastpiece is made to match, with four rows of gemstones (verses 8-13). “The twelve stones corresponded to the names of the sons of Israel. Each stone was engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes” (verse 14). It is tied to the ephod with gold chains and a cord of blue (verses 15-21).
passages.hearers:
The last things to be made are the clothes of the priests. They follow the plan of chapter 28, and the notes there describe each garment and what it meant.

One detail of the craft is new. Verse 3 tells how the gold thread was made: the workers hammered gold into thin sheets and cut it into strips to weave in with the yarn. It is a method known from ancient cloth.

The ephod was a kind of apron or vest. On its shoulders sat two onyx stones cut with the names of the tribes. On the priest's chest was the breastpiece, with twelve gems, one for each tribe. So when the high priest went into the Holy Place he carried the whole people with him, on his shoulders and over his heart. The stones were engraved ‘like a seal’. A seal with a name on it was a mark of who a person was and to whom he belonged.

Which stones were they? No one is sure. The English names in our Bibles are careful guesses, and translations differ.

‘Memorial stones’ does not mean that God might forget. In the Old Testament, to remember is to act for someone. The priest's work was to hold the people before God.

The Urim and Thummim, which were kept in the breastpiece (28:30), are not mentioned here. Perhaps that is because the craftsmen did not make them.

One phrase keeps returning: ‘just as the LORD had commanded Moses’. It marks the making of the garments seven times in this chapter.
passages.later:
Revelation's new Jerusalem has foundations “adorned with every kind of precious stone” (Revelation 21:19), and several of its stones are the same as these.

Hebrews says of Jesus, “we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God” (Hebrews 4:14), and “He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

That line from Aaron to Christ is drawn by the New Testament itself. It does not slight Aaron's service or the worship of Israel. As the notes on Hebrews 8 say, a shadow is real.
passages.asks: The priest carried every tribe by name into God's presence. Ask who carries your name before God, and whose names you carry. And ask what it means to you that you are known to God by name and not as one of a crowd.

passages.t: The robe, the linen, and the gold plate
passages.happening:
“They made the robe of the ephod entirely of blue cloth, the work of a weaver” (verse 22). Around its hem go pomegranates of colored yarn and bells of pure gold, one after the other (verses 24-26).

“For Aaron and his sons they made tunics of fine linen, the work of a weaver” (verse 27), with the turban, the headbands, the undergarments and the sash (verses 28-29).

“They also made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and they engraved on it, like an inscription on a seal: HOLY TO THE LORD” (verse 30). It is tied to the turban with a blue cord (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The blue robe went with the ephod. Its hem rang as the priest moved. The plan said the sound was to be heard when he went in and came out of the sanctuary, ‘so that he will not die’ (28:35). The pomegranate, full of seeds, was a common sign of fruitfulness and life. It appears again on the pillars of Solomon's temple.

Aaron's sons wore plain linen. The high priest wore the gold plate.

The Hebrew word for the plate means a flower or blossom. Verse 30 also calls it ‘the holy crown’. Its words, ‘HOLY TO THE LORD’, were the first thing anyone saw on him. According to 28:38, the plate let the priest bear the guilt that clung even to Israel's holy gifts, so that the gifts would be accepted.

Remember who will wear this. Aaron made the calf. The garments of ‘glory and splendor’ were designed for him before he sinned, and they are finished for him after it. No one in this book serves God because he has earned it.
passages.later:
Zechariah looks to a day when the words on the plate are written on ordinary things: “On that day, HOLY TO THE LORD will be inscribed on the bells of the horses” (Zechariah 14:20).

Peter gives the priests' calling to the whole church: “you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). John sees the risen Christ “dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest” (Revelation 1:13).
passages.asks: The man who made the calf was given garments that said ‘holy to the LORD’. Ask whether you believe God can still use you after your worst failure. And ask what ordinary thing in your life could carry those words.

passages.t: The work finished, and Moses' blessing
passages.happening:
“So all the work for the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting, was completed. The Israelites did everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses” (verse 32).

“Then they brought the tabernacle to Moses” (verse 33): the tent and its frames, the coverings and the veil, the ark and the mercy seat, the table, the lampstand, the gold altar, the bronze altar, the basin, the curtains of the courtyard and the priests' garments (verses 33-41).

“The Israelites had done all the work just as the LORD had commanded Moses. And Moses inspected all the work and saw that they had accomplished it just as the LORD had commanded. So Moses blessed them” (verses 42-43).
passages.hearers:
Everything is brought to Moses, piece by piece, and he looks it over. The list runs through all that has been made since chapter 36.

The people who broke the covenant at the foot of the mountain have now done all that God said, exactly. The chapter says so three more times in these last verses. After the calf, that plain sentence is good news. The relationship has been restored, and it shows in careful obedience.

The ending is written to sound like the end of the creation story. The work ‘was completed’, as the heavens and the earth were completed. Moses ‘saw’ all the work, as God looked on all that he had made. And Moses blessed them, as God blessed his creatures and the seventh day. The tabernacle is presented as a small new world, set in order for God to live in.

The last time Moses came down and looked at what the people had made, he broke the tablets. This time he blesses them.

What remains is for the tent to be set up, and for God himself to come.
passages.later:
Genesis says, “Thus the heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array” (Genesis 2:1), and “God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). “Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (Genesis 2:3).

A prayer that bears Moses' name asks God to do for his people what this chapter shows: “May the favor of the Lord our God rest upon us; establish for us the work of our hands” (Psalm 90:17).
passages.asks: Moses looked at the people's work and blessed them. Ask whether you can receive a blessing on your work, or only see what is wrong with it. And ask what work of your hands you want God to establish.
